title: Rounding Decimals

findings.finding: The halfway-round-up convention is first required before it is stated.
findings.breakdown: In p3-part-d, 5.55 is equally distant from 5.5 and 5.6. The preceding instruction to choose the nearer endpoint cannot resolve this case.
findings.checked: The definition, demonstration and parts a–c supply proximity reasoning but no tie convention. p3-key-idea-2 supplies the convention only after the activity. Solution-only explanations do not supply student-facing teaching.
findings.assumptions: Teacher-led delivery does not establish that an unstated convention has already been supplied.

repair.proposal: Add to p3-part-d: “When a number is exactly halfway between the two endpoints, round to the higher endpoint.”

findings.doneWhen: The halfway convention is available before students answer p3-part-d.

findings.finding: The nearest-whole rounding task for 9.9 is repeated with unchanged number-line givens and no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks require placing 9.9 on the same tenth-divided interval from 9 to 10 and choosing the nearest whole number. The approximation-symbol response does not introduce a different mathematical task.
findings.checked: Compared the complete instructions, value, requested accuracy, endpoints, intervals and midpoint labels. No explicit instructional purpose explains the repeat.
findings.assumptions: The later item is ordinary practice.

repair.proposal: Change p4-q1-b to “6.9 ≈ [blank]”, with a number line from 6 to 7 divided into tenths and labelled at 6, 6.5 and 7. Answer: 7.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure but uses the replacement value and matching number line.

findings.finding: A short sequence could expose the halfway boundary while keeping the bounding whole numbers fixed.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice contains examples on either side of a midpoint but no consecutive numerical run isolating where the rounded answer changes.
findings.checked: The proposed answers are correct under the convention stated in p3-key-idea-2. The sequence uses the number-line method already taught.

repair.proposal: After p4-q1-d, add the single instruction “Predict where the rounded answer will change.” Under the existing rounding instruction, add e: 3.4 ≈ [3]; f: 3.5 ≈ [4]; g: 3.6 ≈ [4], each with the same tenth-divided number line from 3 to 4. Follow with unpatterned part h: 8.2 ≈ [8], with a matching number line from 8 to 9. Only the input position varies in e–g; endpoints, scale and accuracy stay fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The three-part boundary sequence and its unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing instruction.

findings.finding: The table contains two identical tasks rounding 0.152 to one, two and three decimal places.
findings.breakdown: Both rows have the same input, column instructions and required decisions. No explicit comparison or retrieval purpose explains the repetition.
findings.checked: Compared both complete 0.152 rows in p8-q7-response. The proposed replacement gives 0.2, 0.16 and 0.156.
findings.assumptions: Each row is an individual practice task under the shared table instruction.

repair.proposal: Keep the first 0.152 row. Replace the second with 0.156. Its answers, in column order, are 0.2, 0.16 and 0.156.

findings.doneWhen: Only one 0.152 row remains, and the replacement preserves all three precision columns.

findings.finding: A controlled sequence could isolate the critical-digit threshold, including carrying into the whole-number place.
findings.breakdown: The original proposed run changes both discarded positions. Fixing the thousandths digit makes the hundredths digit the sole varying feature.
findings.checked: The revised sequence uses the critical-digit method and carrying already supplied by p5-method-block and p5-guided-e-node. All proposed answers are correct.

repair.proposal: After p7-q5-h, add the single instruction “Predict which answers will be equal before rounding.” Under the existing instruction to round to 1 decimal place, add i: 7.931 → 7.9; j: 7.941 → 7.9; k: 7.951 → 8.0; l: 7.961 → 8.0. Follow with unpatterned part m: 3.684 → 3.7. In i–l only the hundredths digit varies; the retained digits, thousandths digit and requested accuracy stay fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The run varies only the critical digit and includes the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: A follow-up using ten identical boxes would show accumulated rounding error changing the final two-decimal-place answer.
findings.breakdown: For one box, both routes round to 39.06 cm². For ten boxes, the early-rounded route gives 390.60 cm² while rounding only at the end gives 390.62 cm².
findings.checked: The exact one-box total is 39.0622 cm². Multiplying by ten gives 390.622 cm², which rounds to 390.62 cm²; the difference between the rounded totals is 0.02 cm². Calculator use is explicit in the existing question.
findings.assumptions: The ten boxes are identical to the existing box.

repair.proposal: After p10-q13-comparison-node, add optional parts: (a) “Using the early-rounded total for one box, find the total net area for ten identical boxes.” Answer: 390.60 cm². (b) “Using the exact total for one box, find the total net area for ten identical boxes, rounding only at the end to two decimal places.” Answer: 390.622 cm² ≈ 390.62 cm². (c) “How much smaller is the answer in part (a) than the rounded answer in part (b)?” Answer: 0.02 cm².

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up compares the two routes for ten boxes using the existing totals.

findings.finding: Parts b and d repeat the classification of the same decimal in the same ellipsis notation without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Displaying one additional repeated 5 changes neither the given infinite decimal nor the classification task. Part c changes notation, but no instruction gives the repeated ellipsis task a retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared the complete prompts of b and d and their surrounding parts. Both denote 0.555… and require the same terminating-or-recurring decision. The proposed replacement is recurring.
findings.assumptions: The ellipses indicate continued repetition of 5 in both original parts.

repair.proposal: Keep p12-q3-b. Change p12-q3-d to “0.6666666666…”. Answer: recurring.

findings.doneWhen: Part d preserves the classification task and representation but uses a different decimal value.

findings.finding: The classification of pi requires its non-recurrence, but the question supplies only non-termination and a finite prefix.
findings.breakdown: Neither a never-ending expansion nor the absence of an obvious pattern in 100 digits establishes that no block eventually repeats. Using these as justification risks teaching an invalid classification rule.
findings.checked: p11-information-block distinguishes recurrence by repetition forever. p12-q1-root defines non-recurrence, and p12-q2-b explicitly supplies the absence of a repeating pattern. No preceding teaching supplies that fact for pi or a method to prove it.
findings.assumptions: Pi's non-recurrence is not assumed prior knowledge; familiarity with pi in circle measurement does not establish this property.

repair.proposal: Before the classification question, add: “It is known that pi's decimal digits continue forever and never settle into a repeating block. The displayed digits alone cannot establish this.”

findings.doneWhen: Students can justify the classification using a supplied property of the infinite expansion.

findings.finding: A shorter follow-up using thirds could expose how adding rounded recurring decimals can differ from the exact sum.
findings.breakdown: Three copies of the rounded value 0.33 total 0.99, whereas three exact thirds total 1. This directly connects recurring decimals with the booklet’s rounding work.
findings.checked: One third rounds to 0.33 at two decimal places; 3 × 0.33 = 0.99 and 3 × 1/3 = 1. The task requires only rounding, recurring decimals and elementary arithmetic already available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: These are optional follow-up parts using the fraction in p13-q5-a.

repair.proposal: After p13-q5-d, add optional parts: (e) “Round 1/3 to two decimal places.” Answer: 0.33. (f) “Add three copies of your rounded value.” Answer: 0.99. (g) “Find the exact sum of three copies of 1/3.” Answer: 1. (h) “Explain why the rounded-value total is smaller than the exact sum.” Expected answer: Each 0.33 is smaller than 1/3, so adding three rounded values gives 0.99, which is 0.01 below 1.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares an exact sum with the sum of rounded values using separate, single-question parts.

findings.finding: Explore how different repeating-block lengths can represent the same decimal.
findings.breakdown: Expanding the notation lets students explain its meaning and distinguish equivalent blocks from a changed pattern.
findings.checked: The three proposed blocks all generate 0.272727272727…. Every finite repeating block starting immediately after the decimal point that generates this expansion consists of a positive whole number of copies of 27. The block 277 generates 0.277277277…, a different value. Only expansion and recurring notation taught in topic 3 are required.
findings.assumptions: The repeating block starts immediately after the decimal point, as in the supplied expressions.

repair.proposal: After p14-q6-root, offer: “Do 0.\overline{27}, 0.\overline{2727} and 0.\overline{272727} represent the same number? Write their first twelve decimal digits to explain. Describe every repeating block that can replace 27 without changing this decimal. Would 0.\overline{277} also work?” Expected answer: the first three all expand to 0.272727272727…. Any positive whole number of consecutive copies of 27 works; 277 does not.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks students to explain equivalence through expansion and rejects the changed block correctly.

protectedGroups.observation: Nearest-tenth rounding contrasts inputs below, above and exactly at the midpoint.
protectedGroups.varies: The input's position relative to the midpoint.
protectedGroups.invariant: Requested accuracy and hundredth-sized intervals between neighbouring tenths.

protectedGroups.observation: Nearest-hundredth rounding requires choosing either the lower or higher endpoint.
protectedGroups.varies: The input's side of the midpoint.

protectedGroups.observation: Repeated-looking digits do not make a finite decimal recurring; bar notation and an ellipsis specify continued repetition.
protectedGroups.varies: Finite length and the notation specifying whether repetition continues forever.
protectedGroups.invariant: The digits follow the repeating block 85.

protectedGroups.observation: Only the recurring digit receives the dot, even when a whole-number part or a non-repeating decimal prefix is present.
protectedGroups.varies: Whole-number part and the presence and value of a non-repeating prefix.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the rounding place changes which digit controls the decision.
protectedGroups.varies: Requested precision and corresponding critical digit.

protectedGroups.observation: Intermediate rounding changes the accumulated value even when final rounding produces the same displayed total.
protectedGroups.invariant: The box, dimensions, face areas and final requested precision.
